# The Depression and the Stakes of Interpretation {#sec-3-08}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1929–1939
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** What happens when the governing story breaks down?

**The answer.** Competence stops counting. Hoover was arguably the most
administratively accomplished man ever to hold the presidency and the Depression
destroyed him, because the crisis was not an engineering problem and he governed
it as one. The 1930s established that the winning story about what institutions
are for determines the shape of regulation, labour law, and capital formation
for a generation.

**The mechanism.** The legitimacy layer failing. Every prior chapter has shown
legitimacy being manufactured; this one shows what happens when it cannot be.
The New Deal is a competing account of what institutions are for, and it wins —
which means California's elite spends the next fifty years learning to fight on
the terrain of narrative rather than administration.

**The key fact.** Hoover's response to the Depression was more interventionist
than any previous president's — the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, public
works, the Federal Home Loan Bank system. He lost anyway, and his name became a
synonym for doing nothing. The gap between the record and the reputation is the
chapter's subject.

**The human anchor.** Hoover, the logistics genius who fed Belgium, unable to
explain America to itself. The same skills, a different kind of problem.

**Excluded voices.** The people the interpretive fight was about: the Dust Bowl
migrants arriving in California, the farm workers whose organising was met with
force — material the next chapter's Steinbeck reference has already established.
Cross-reference rather than duplicate.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that interpretation rather than administration
decides legitimacy crises by showing the most technically capable president of
the era lose office having implemented more intervention than his predecessors.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Hooverville is a word that did political work the record does not support, and
the chapter begins there, because the gap between what Hoover did and what his
name came to mean is its subject.

He was arguably the most administratively accomplished man ever to hold the
presidency. He had fed a continent, run a federal department as a national
clearing house, and built a reputation as the era's outstanding manager of
complex systems. His response to the Depression was more interventionist than
any predecessor's: the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, the Federal Home Loan
Bank system, expanded public works. The chapter gives that case at full
strength, because the argument requires it.

And it failed, because the crisis was not an engineering problem and he governed
it as one. He kept solving the wrong problem correctly. What had broken in 1929
was not only prices but the account of why the winners had won, and the country
was asking a question about legitimacy to which administrative competence was
not an answer.

Roosevelt supplied the competing story first and the policy programme second.
The New Deal is best understood in this chapter as an interpretation of what
institutions are for, and the chapter's structural claim is that the winning
interpretation determined the shape of labour law, securities regulation, and
capital formation for the next fifty years. Ideas were the decisive assets of
the decade, not factories.

California's exposure was acute: migration into the state, agricultural labour
conflicts met with force, and a growing dependence on federal water and public
works.

The chapter ends with Hoover in Palo Alto, a defeated president assembling an
intellectual apparatus for a comeback. It arrives in 1980 with somebody else's
name on it, and Act IV chapter 10 collects the payment.

The lesson California's elite absorbed is that administrative competence is not
sufficient, and that whoever loses the argument loses everything downstream of
it. They did not make the mistake again.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
What happens when the governing story breaks down?
:::

Hooverville.

The word attached itself to the shanty settlements that appeared on the edges of
American cities after 1929, and it did more political damage than any speech of
the period. It was also, as a description of the man's actual policy, close to
the opposite of the truth.

The gap between what Herbert Hoover did and what his name came to mean is this
chapter's subject, because that gap is where the twentieth century turned.

## The most qualified man available

By any reasonable assessment in 1928, Hoover was the best-prepared person ever
to enter the American presidency.

He had run a global engineering practice. He had fed occupied Belgium through
four years of blockade, and much of central and eastern Europe after the
armistice. He had directed the American food supply during the war. He had spent
eight years running the Commerce Department as a national coordinating body, and
he had managed the federal response to the Mississippi flood of 1927, which was
the largest domestic relief operation the country had yet mounted.

He was the country's designated organiser. He was elected by a very large margin
on precisely that reputation.

## What he actually did

The chapter has to give this at full strength, because the argument depends on
his competence being real.

Hoover's response to the Depression was more interventionist than that of any
previous American president facing an economic contraction. He expanded federal
public works. He created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation in 1932 to lend
to banks, railroads, and other institutions, which was an unprecedented
insertion of federal credit into the private economy and which the Roosevelt
administration subsequently kept and expanded. He signed the Federal Home Loan
Bank Act to support mortgage lending. He convened business leaders and secured
commitments to maintain wages, which held for a considerable period.

He also did things that made it worse — signing the Smoot-Hawley tariff, and
supporting a tax increase in 1932 in pursuit of a balanced budget — and the
chapter should say so. But the picture of a president who believed in doing
nothing is not supported by the record. He believed in doing a great deal,
through voluntary coordination and indirect federal support, and he did it.

It was not enough, and more importantly it was not the thing being asked for.

## Solving the wrong problem correctly

Hoover approached the Depression as an engineering and logistics problem,
because that is what he was superbly good at and because every previous crisis
of his career had been one.

Belgium was a logistics problem: food existed, people needed it, and the task
was to move it through a blockade and account for it. The Mississippi flood was
a logistics problem. Wartime food supply was a logistics problem.

The Depression was not. It was a crisis of confidence, expectation, and
legitimacy, and by 1931 it had become a crisis about whether the American
economic order deserved to continue. What had broken in 1929 was not only
prices. It was the account of why the people at the top were at the top — an
account that, as chapter 3 described, had recently been given a biological
formulation by respectable scientists.

You cannot restore confidence by convening a committee, and you cannot answer a
question about desert with a credit facility. Hoover kept producing correct
technical answers to a question nobody was asking.

The Bonus Army made the mismatch visible. In the summer of 1932 tens of
thousands of unemployed veterans camped in Washington seeking early payment of a
promised bonus. The administration's handling of it ended with the army clearing
the camps with cavalry and tanks under MacArthur, and the newsreels of that were
the end of Hoover's political life. The administrative question — whether the
bonus should be accelerated — was arguable. The image was not.

## Roosevelt as interpretation

Franklin Roosevelt's advantage in 1932 was not a superior programme. Much of the
early New Deal was improvised, some of it contradicted the rest, and a good deal
of it was continuous with what Hoover had already begun.

His advantage was that he supplied an interpretation. He told the country that
the crisis had causes rather than being weather, that those causes were located
in the conduct of finance and the structure of the economy, and that government
existed to act on them. It was an account of what institutions are for, and
against it Hoover had a set of measures.

The winning interpretation then determined the structure of American capitalism
for fifty years. Securities regulation and the separation of investment from
commercial banking. Federal deposit insurance. Collective bargaining rights and
the labour law that followed. Social insurance. Federal mortgage guarantees,
with the redlining maps described in chapter 3 built into them. Agricultural
price supports, which in California flowed overwhelmingly to large operators
rather than to the labour force Steinbeck was writing about.

Ideas were the decisive assets of the decade. Not factories, not gold, and
certainly not administrative capability.

## California

The state's exposure was acute and specific. Migration from the Dust Bowl states
brought several hundred thousand people into California looking for agricultural
work that did not exist in the quantity required, into a labour system built on
the century-long sequence of recruited and discarded workforces described in Act
II. Wages collapsed. Organising was met with force, by growers' associations
operating with local law enforcement, in episodes that ran through the entire
decade.

And California became dependent on federal money in a way it had not been before
— water projects, public works, and eventually defence. That dependence is the
bridge into the second half of this act.

## The dam

There is a monument to the other half of Hoover's career, and it is three
hundred and seventy miles from Palo Alto on the Colorado River.

The dam at Black Canyon was authorised in 1928 and built between 1931 and 1936,
and Hoover's role in it began long before the presidency: as Secretary of
Commerce he had chaired the negotiations that produced the Colorado River
Compact of 1922, the agreement among seven states that made the project legally
possible by allocating the river's water among them.

That compact is one of the most consequential documents in the history of the
American West. It divided the river between an upper and a lower basin on the
basis of flow measurements taken during an unusually wet period, which means it
allocated more water than the river reliably carries — a structural error that
the region has been managing ever since and is managing now.

The dam itself did what large infrastructure does in this book. It made southern
California's growth possible by supplying water and power, and the power
contracts that financed it went substantially to Los Angeles. Public money and
federal authority produced an asset whose benefits accrued to specific private
and municipal interests, allocated by a formula negotiated in a room.

It was named for Hoover, renamed by the Roosevelt administration, and renamed
for him again by Congress in 1947.

The relevance to this chapter is that the same man, in the same decade,
succeeded completely at a logistics and negotiation problem and failed
completely at an interpretive one. The skills were not deficient. They were the
wrong skills for what was being asked, and there is no evidence he ever accepted
that.

## Palo Alto

Hoover left office in March 1933 and returned to Stanford, where he lived on the
campus in a house on San Juan Hill and spent the next thirty years building the
Institution that carried his name into something with a point of view.

A defeated president assembling an intellectual apparatus is a familiar figure
and usually a pathetic one. This one worked. The Institution grew, acquired
permanent scholars, and became a base from which a particular set of economic
and foreign policy arguments could be developed and sustained across decades in
which they were entirely out of fashion.

The payoff arrives in 1980, with somebody else's name on the ballot. Act IV
chapter 10 collects it.

What California's elite learned in the 1930s is that administrative competence
is not sufficient, and that whoever loses the argument about what institutions
are for loses everything downstream of it. They did not make the mistake twice.
